cards.text: This is a psalm of Asaph. Back in David's day, Asaph was the chief Levite leading worship before the ark (1 Chronicles 16:4-5). Here he's praying straight to God, and he skips the small talk: the nations have invaded God's inheritance.

cards.question: The nations have invaded. What does Asaph tell God they did to His holy temple?
Asaph tells God the invaders left the city of Jerusalem standing.

cards.text: Then it gets heavy, friend. The bodies of God's servants have been left out as food for the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth.

cards.question: Blood has been poured out like water all around Jerusalem. What does Asaph say there's no one left to do?
With Jerusalem in ruins, how are the people living around Israel treating them?

answers.text: They rush in to help them

cards.text: Then Asaph stops describing and asks God, "How long, O LORD?" Friend, I asked that every night in the junk drawer, except I asked the dead batteries next to me, and they had NO answers.

cards.question: Asaph's next question is about God's anger. Will You be angry ___?
Asaph also asks whether God's jealousy will burn like fire.

cards.text: Then the prayer turns. Asaph asks God to pour out His wrath.

cards.question: Asaph asks God to pour out His wrath. On whom?

answers.text: The nations that don't acknowledge Him
The priests who left the temple
The leaders who lost the city

cards.question: Asaph says those nations have devoured God's people and devastated their homeland.

cards.text: Now Asaph turns the spotlight off the nations and onto his own people. And he doesn't pretend they're spotless.

cards.question: What does Asaph ask God NOT to do to His people?
Since his people are brought low, Asaph asks God to take His time showing compassion.

cards.text: Then Asaph asks the God of their salvation to help them, deliver them and atone for their sins. That's not asking for a small favor, friend, that's asking for a FULL rescue.

cards.question: Asaph asks God to deliver them and atone for their sins for the sake of His ___.
Asaph doesn't want the nations asking a certain question about God's people. What is it?

cards.text: Asaph asks God to make His vengeance for the blood of His servants known among the nations, right before their eyes. Then his prayer turns to the ones still suffering.

cards.question: Asaph prays, May the groans of the ___ reach You.
Asaph asks God to preserve those condemned to death by the strength of His arm.

cards.text: Then Asaph asks God to pay their neighbors back for their reproach. Not double, friend. SEVENFOLD.

cards.question: Asaph wants the neighbors paid back for their reproach. Who does he say they hurled it at?

cards.text: And Asaph doesn't end in the rubble. He ends with a promise about what God's people will do next.

cards.question: What does Asaph promise God's people will do?

answers.text: Thank Him forever and declare His praise
Rebuild His temple stone by stone
Guard Jerusalem by day and night

cards.question: In that last line, Asaph calls God's people the sheep of His pasture.

cards.text: From generation to generation, friend. That praise is gonna outlast every oven in my bakery, and DEFINITELY my old junk drawer.

findings.problem: The card introduces the psalm's author with 'Back in David's day, Asaph was the chief Levite leading worship before the ark (1 Chronicles 16:4-5).' Psalm 79 describes the temple defiled and Jerusalem in rubble, which comes long after David's day. The card ties the 'Asaph' of the superscription to David's Asaph, but Psalm 79 never makes that link. The docs require introducing new people simply and leaving open what the text leaves open. They don't say how to introduce a psalm author when the superscription's name may refer to someone other than the person by that name elsewhere in Scripture.
findings.question: How should Papa Dorin introduce 'Asaph' in a psalm whose events come after David's lifetime? Should he cite 1 Chronicles 16:4-5 as who Asaph is, say only 'a psalm of Asaph' with no identification, or use a set wording for Asaph psalms (for example, Asaph or his line of worship leaders)?

findings.problem: The joke invents a new backstory habit: that Papa Dorin asked 'How long?' every night in the junk drawer and put the question to the dead batteries. The backstory says he went quiet in the drawer ('He didn't talk much'). Jokes may make up small moments around his bakery, not new drawer history.

rule.text: His own world isn't Bible fact. His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them. His jokes can make up small moments and habits around his bakery.

findings.problem: This is a 'who' question, but the wrong answers 'The priests who left the temple' and 'The leaders who lost the city' are invented groups, not real details from somewhere in the Bible.

rule.text: For who, which thing and where questions, wrong answers are real details from somewhere in the Bible, like Joppa when the right answer is Tarshish.

findings.problem: The blank asks the baker to supply the word 'name' in 'for the sake of His ___.' Card 4 retold verse 9 but left out both mentions of God's name, so nothing earlier lets the baker reason to 'name' over 'temple' or 'servants'. This is guessing the wording of the line.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The card says God's vengeance should be made known among the nations 'right before their eyes'. In context, 'their' reads as the nations' eyes. The BSB says 'Before our eyes', meaning the eyes of the psalmist and God's people. The retelling changes whose eyes they are.

rule.text: Retelling: Papa Dorin can retell in his own words and fill in what the text clearly implies. Scene-setting details are fine. He never says anything the text shows is wrong.

findings.problem: Stop 2 opens with the same card pattern as Stop 1: story, multiple choice, true or false. Both stops also keep using the same move: a story card, then a multiple choice card, then a true or false card on the same verse (Stop 1 cards 1-3; Stop 2 cards 1-3 and 12-14). The order of question types follows a repeated pattern.

rule.text: No formula. Which question type comes next, the order the types come in and where a blank falls are chosen naturally for each card. They never follow a pattern. No stop repeats another stop's pattern, and no type dominates a stop by a wide margin.
